routes.description: Establish that Christianity offers humanity the brighter future by showing that its worldview grounds and sustains moral formation, rights-bearing institutions, social cooperation, meaning, and truth-seeking across generations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christianity is shown to provide credible foundations and durable mechanisms for preserving human dignity, free institutions, social health, purposeful agency, and intellectual progress better than a society detached from those foundations.

motionBridge.description: Connect Christianity's claimed truth and formative effects to a comparatively brighter, freer, healthier, and more sustainable human future.

centralBridges.description: Show how Christian anthropology and historical formation ground human equality, rights, limited government, and protection of vulnerable people.
Show that Christian participation, motivation, community practices, and demographic continuity sustain social cooperation and liberal institutions over time.
Defend Christianity's coherence and evidential credibility while explaining how Christian commitments support reliable inquiry and scientific institutions.
Show that equal civil rights, practical cooperation, and appropriately bounded conscience protections can coexist within a Christian social framework.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how Christian hope, purpose, and moral narrative motivate ordinary and disadvantaged people toward responsibility and social improvement.
Answer specific objections concerning suffering, agency, scripture, historical causation, and contested applications of religious liberty.

routes.description: Establish that humanism offers humanity the brighter future by showing that reason, shared human interests, and political secularism support moral responsibility, healthy societies, equal rights, truth-seeking, and pluralistic freedom without Christian foundations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if humanism is shown to furnish inclusive moral and political commitments, credible methods of inquiry, and sustainable social arrangements while Christianity's asserted necessity, truth, and entitlement to public privilege remain unestablished.

motionBridge.description: Connect humanist moral autonomy, evidence-based inquiry, and state neutrality to a comparatively healthier, freer, and more inclusive human future.

centralBridges.description: Show that moral responsibility and shared commitments can rest on religiously neutral reasons accessible to Christians, non-Christians, and nonbelievers alike.
Show that healthy secular and non-Christian societies undermine claims that Christianity is necessary for decency, cooperation, institutional stability, or future flourishing.
Test the coherence, morality, and evidential support of Christian claims that would need to be credible before Christianity could serve as society's foundation.
Show that political secularism protects equal citizenship by withholding religious privilege and evaluating conscience claims without favoring their religious origin.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether Christianity deserves unique causal credit for rights, reform, science, and other achievements produced within historically Christian societies.
Test whether secularization causes harmful fertility decline and whether lower fertility or demographic change establishes Christianity's comparative necessity.

sections.title: Moral foundations, human dignity, and historical inheritance
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing whether Christianity or humanism can ground moral responsibility and human worth, and whether the West's rights tradition depends on specifically Christian formation.

sections.title: Christian truth, evidence, suffering, and human agency
sections.rationale: Christianity's suitability as a future foundation depends partly on the coherence and evidential support of its claims about God, salvation, suffering, scripture, souls, and free agency.

sections.title: Social health, motivation, and generational sustainability
sections.rationale: Claims about charity, community, meaning, secular social outcomes, fertility, and inherited religious capital directly test which outlook can sustain flourishing institutions across generations.

sections.title: Equal rights, political secularism, and conscience
sections.rationale: The competing approaches to state neutrality, religious privilege, nondiscrimination, sexuality, and conscience exemptions bear directly on human rights and pluralistic freedom.

sections.title: Science, institutional autonomy, and intellectual progress
sections.rationale: The historical origins and institutional conditions of scientific inquiry matter to the debate's truth dimension and to each worldview's capacity to support continuing human advancement.

routes.description: Establish Christian theism through a cumulative case combining a finite cosmic beginning, cosmic fine-tuning, moral and experiential grounds, the resurrection, and an account of suffering compatible with divine goodness.
routes.successCriteria: This route succeeds if the supporting considerations jointly warrant belief in God and Christian theism, while the proposed reasons for permitting suffering prevent animal pain and other evil from defeating that cumulative inference.

motionBridge.description: The combined public and experiential grounds must warrant the conclusion that God exists and that Christian theism remains credible.

centralBridges.description: The philosophical and scientific case must support a finite cosmic past requiring a transcendent cause.
Life-permitting constants must be sufficiently improbable by accident for intelligent selection to provide the better explanation.
Resurrection evidence and personal experience must connect generic theistic explanation to specifically Christian belief.
Divine goodness and power must remain compatible with evolutionary animal suffering and the wider distribution of evil.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The account of actual infinity and temporal becoming must sustain the claimed asymmetry between a beginningless past and an endless future.
Human limits concerning feasible worlds and greater goods must justify withholding the inference that apparently gratuitous suffering is genuinely gratuitous.

routes.description: Withhold assent from Christian theism by challenging the finite-past and fine-tuning inferences and by arguing that animal suffering, its distribution, and divine involvement are evidence against an all-loving Christian God.
routes.successCriteria: This route succeeds if the cosmological or fine-tuning case does not establish its required divine conclusion, or if suffering remains materially less expected under the personally concerned and morally perfect God asserted by Christian theism.

motionBridge.description: Unresolved inferential gaps and counterevidence must leave the existence of the Christian God insufficiently warranted.

centralBridges.description: Scientific uncertainty and disputes about actual infinity, temporal units, and theories of time must undercut the claim that the universe began.
The fine-tuning inference must fail to show that divine intention explains the life-permitting constants and their hostile background conditions.
Evolutionary animal suffering and its apparently arbitrary distribution must count as evidence against an all-loving and powerful God.
The moral character and saving concern attributed to the Christian God must make suffering relevant beyond the existence of an indifferent first cause.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Coherent alternatives involving non-sentient animals or different creative means must challenge claims that suffering-producing conditions were necessary.
Appeals to limited moral understanding must remain consistent with reliance on human moral awareness in arguments for objective morality.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Actual Infinity, and the Nature of Time
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal clash over whether philosophy, astrophysics, and thermodynamics establish a finite cosmic past, including the actual-infinity and temporal-asymmetry premises needed by the cosmological argument.

sections.title: Cosmic Fine-Tuning and Intelligent Selection
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether life-permitting constants favor intentional selection over accident or brute necessity and whether the background conditions for matter fit the proposed creative intention.

sections.title: Animal Suffering, Theodicy, and Feasible Worlds
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether evolutionary animal suffering is necessary for salvific goods, whether less harmful worlds are feasible, and whether limited human knowledge blocks judgments of gratuitous evil.

sections.title: Divine Goodness, Moral Knowledge, and the Distribution of Evil
sections.rationale: This issue connects suffering's severity and distribution to the attributes of the Christian God and tests whether skeptical appeals about divine reasons remain consistent with moral arguments and scriptural claims.

sections.title: Christian Identification, Experience, and Cumulative Warrant
sections.rationale: This issue examines the steps from generic creator arguments to Christian theism through resurrection and inward experience, together with the objection that evidence against a saving, personally concerned God remains relevant to the cumulative case.

routes.description: Establish the anti-realist burden by denying that realism enjoys a defensible common-sense, historical, or semantic presumption and by showing that a substantive anti-realist alternative survives the principal conceptual objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the alleged realist advantages depend on unreliable attribution, contested semantic assumptions, or projection of specialist categories, while anti-realism remains a coherent position with consequences distinguishable from rival relativist accounts.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, and semantic considerations do not establish a presumptive advantage for moral realism over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that ordinary or remembered pre-philosophical outlooks cannot reliably be classified using determinate contemporary metaethical categories.
Show that historical convergence claims must overcome projection, translation, source-selection, cultural-contact, and specialist-competence problems.
Articulate a genuinely metaethical anti-realist alternative whose semantic and practical commitments remain distinct from agent-relative obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify what surveys, linguistic use, memory, and behavior can establish about moral thought without treating them as direct tests of moral reality.
Show that interpretive or epistemic mediation does not uniquely discredit anti-realist positions when comparable access problems arise elsewhere.

routes.description: Establish the realist burden by defending common-sense or historical evidence for an objective conception of value and by showing that the proposed anti-realist distinctions do not defeat the resulting realist presumption.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suitably competent pre-philosophical or cross-era sources provide credible evidence of objective-value commitments and if the anti-realist alternative either collapses into a perspectival variant or fails to displace that evidential presumption.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, or semantic evidence supplies moral realism with a meaningful presumptive advantage over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Identify a defensible common-sense evidential population despite the limitations of unreflective street-level surveys and raw response variation.
Establish that sufficiently comparable philosophical or intellectual traditions converge on objectively intended value claims despite substantive disagreement.
Show that agent and appraiser relativism share an underlying perspectival structure sufficient to limit the claimed semantic or metaphysical contrast.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for heterogeneous reports through competence, motivation, ignorance, or other factors that need not undermine an initial realist seeming.
Explain how an agent's interpretation of external standards bears on the claimed practical separation between relativist positions.

sections.title: Empirical Semantics and Metaphysical Scope
sections.rationale: The parties must delimit what evidence about linguistic use, psychology, surveys, or behavior can establish about ordinary meaning and whether any such finding bears directly on moral reality.

sections.title: Common Sense and Pre-Theoretical Outlooks
sections.rationale: A claimed common-sense advantage depends on identifying competent evidence of pre-theoretical commitments and resolving whether memory, reflection, pragmatic effects, and response variation permit reliable attribution.

sections.title: Historical Convergence and Metaethical Attribution
sections.rationale: The historical branch of the motion turns on whether cross-era intellectual traditions provide comparable evidence of objective-value commitments despite projection, translation, source-selection, and cultural-independence concerns.

sections.title: Agent and Appraiser Relativism
sections.rationale: The conceptual viability of the anti-realist alternative depends on whether these forms of relativism differ in semantic, metaphysical, and normative structure or merely redescribe one perspectival position.

sections.title: Normative Conflict and Epistemic Mediation
sections.rationale: Conflicting standards and first-person interpretation test the practical implications of the relativist distinction and whether access limitations create a distinctive problem for anti-realism.

routes.description: Establish that ethics requires objective moral facts, universally binding obligations, human worth, and reliable moral cognition, and that a good personal creator provides a more adequate foundation for those features than goal-dependent secular humanism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective morality requires a transcendent ground with authority, theism explains human value and access to moral truth, and secular humanism cannot make its welfare commitments binding on dissenters or reliably exclude destructive goals.

motionBridge.description: Show that God supplies the ontological and authoritative foundation required for ethics while secular humanism supplies only conditional guidance toward adopted goals.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective goodness and universal obligations require a nonphysical, humanity-transcending ground possessing moral authority.
Explain how creation in God's image grounds intrinsic human worth, rights, and duties toward other persons.
Show that divine creation can make moral faculties fallibly truth-directed, whereas evolutionary and social conditioning alone explain useful attitudes without establishing their truth.
Demonstrate that welfare-based rules remain conditional on accepting the relevant goal and cannot bind dissenters or rule out harmful programs merely labeled as well-being.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for the practical motivational force of seeing persons as bearers of God-given value and obligations.
Distinguish the claimed theistic foundation from disputed religious applications and test whether historical misconduct undermines either proposed foundation.

routes.description: Establish that ethics can proceed from shared human interests, sentient consequences, empathy, reciprocity, and revisable evidence-based inquiry, while showing that positing God does not by itself identify goodness, derive obligations, resolve disagreement, or provide an actionable ethical system.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if human flourishing and social interdependence support non-arbitrary moral evaluation and correction without intrinsic cosmic commands, while the asserted divine ground remains unsupported, underspecified, or subject to equivalent motivational and interpretive problems.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular humanism provides usable goals and corrective methods for ethics without requiring a demonstrated divine lawgiver or intrinsic universe-wide value.

centralBridges.description: Ground better and worse conduct in objective facts about harm, flourishing, unavoidable social participation, and the consequences of available choices.
Explain how evidence, internal consistency, discussion, and correction can expose harmful means and improve fallible moral judgments without reducing morality to majority opinion.
Justify concern for persons through relational value, empathy, reciprocity, shared vulnerability, and broadly understood mutual interests.
Require the theistic account to demonstrate God's goodness and authority and derive usable obligations rather than defining God as goodness or appealing to disputed interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that God does not necessarily motivate indifferent or opportunistic actors and that improved conduct from a belief does not establish the belief's truth or foundational status.
Explain how human institutions can pursue justice through due process, proportionate intervention, and collective assessment of threats.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: Addresses whether objective moral facts and universal obligations require a transcendent personal ground, whether divine goodness and authority are demonstrated, and whether identifying goodness with God explains or assumes the required foundation.

sections.title: Flourishing, Consequences, and Binding Obligation
sections.rationale: Covers the central dispute over whether shared concern for well-being, physical consequences, and unavoidable social participation generate genuine obligations or only instrumental rules conditional on an adopted goal.

sections.title: Human Value, Rights, and Cooperation
sections.rationale: Compares image-of-God accounts of intrinsic worth with secular accounts based on relational value, empathy, reciprocity, shared interests, and the significance of human lives and relationships.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Disagreement, and Correction
sections.rationale: Examines whether moral cognition is better grounded as divinely truth-directed or as fallible inquiry using evidence, consequences, consistency, education, and revision to identify and correct error.

sections.title: Motivation, Atrocity, and Practical Application
sections.rationale: Tests how each foundation addresses indifference, opportunism, transformation, destructive ideologies, religious interpretation, justice, and intervention without treating motivation or historical labels as sufficient proof of moral truth.

routes.description: Establish consciousness as the sole immediate ontological datum, reject nonconscious emergence as an explanation of experience, and show that a universal mental foundation can preserve objective structure, causal order, and scientific tractability.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if consciousness is shown to require no reduction to a nonexperiential substrate, while the proposed consciousness-first ontology accounts for observer-independent reality, differentiated subjects, regular causation, and nonspatiotemporal structure.

motionBridge.description: Connect the irreducibility of experience and the explanatory adequacy of universal subjectivity to the conclusion that consciousness is reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Show why descriptions of nonconscious physical quantities cannot entail experiential qualities and why positing strong emergence does not close that explanatory gap.
Explain how an external mental reality can remain observer-independent and appear as a stable physical world through perceptual representation and dissociative boundaries.
Ground causal power, differentiation, and natural regularities in the intrinsic dispositions and excitation modes of universal subjectivity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the constructed narrative self from consciousness itself so that rejecting a persistent personal agent does not eliminate experience.
Account for structure beyond fundamental spacetime through meaning-bearing cognitive or semantic relations.

routes.description: Separate rejection of materialist emergence from acceptance of idealism, develop a representation-based neutral monism, and require any consciousness-first ontology to explain structured order, boundaries, causal differentiation, and phenomenal character.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a neutral representational basis can accommodate phenomenal character without treating consciousness as universal substance, while idealism's mental-substrate designation leaves indispensable explanatory work unresolved.

motionBridge.description: Connect the sufficiency of neutral monism and the unresolved explanatory commitments of idealism to denial that consciousness must be reality's ontological foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that rejecting matter-to-consciousness emergence does not by itself select analytic idealism over other nonmaterialist ontologies.
Locate phenomenal character in representations without requiring a separate physical organism, unified self, or universal conscious substance.
Require an account of how a designated mental substrate produces boundaries, predictive representations, structured order, and differentiated causal relations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether information integration supplies an explanatory connection to subjective experience rather than only an empirical correlation.
Use experiences lacking ordinary selfhood, space, or time to examine which features an adequate fundamental ontology must explain.

sections.title: Ontological Starting Point and the Emergence Gap
sections.rationale: This issue tests the principal inference from consciousness as an immediate datum and the explanatory gap of strong emergence to a consciousness-first ontology, including whether that inference excludes neutral alternatives.

sections.title: Objective Reality, Boundaries, and Natural Order
sections.rationale: A viable route must explain how observer-independent structure, perceptual representation, embodied boundaries, evolution, and stable causal regularities arise under its proposed ontology.

sections.title: Representation, Self-Models, and Phenomenal Character
sections.rationale: The dispute over whether phenomenal character belongs to representations, consciousness itself, or a persistent subject bears directly on whether neutral monism suffices or idealism is required.

sections.title: Integrated Information and Causal Existence
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether information integration merely predicts reports or supports claims about subjective viewpoints, self-existing complexes, and the location of causal power.

sections.title: Universal Subjectivity, Differentiation, and Nonspatiotemporal Structure
sections.rationale: The proposed universal subject must account for differentiated experiences and causal order without relying on a personal self, while also explaining structure when ordinary space and time are not fundamental.

routes.description: Establish a physical resurrection as the historically reasonable explanation of Jesus's death, the early bodily-resurrection proclamation, reported individual and group encounters, and the claimed absence of his body.
routes.successCriteria: Connect testimony, bodily continuity, witness conduct, and the tomb into a coherent resurrection explanation while identifying relevant differences from rival miracle traditions and accounting for proposed natural alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined historical considerations make Jesus's physical resurrection a reasonable conclusion relative to the alternatives under discussion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the earliest testimony and later narratives concern encounters with the physically continuous, crucified Jesus rather than only visions or disembodied survival.
Establish a historically usable missing-body or empty-tomb datum and explain why reburial, theft, or related burial hypotheses do not exhaust the combined evidence.
Connect individual and group encounter reports, conversions, and early proclamation to a single resurrection explanation of the movement's central claim.
Apply a consistent evidential framework to rival miracle claims while identifying differences relevant to testimony, incentives, expectations, corroboration, and background knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use danger, persistence, and costly proclamation to establish informed sincerity without treating suffering by itself as proof of resurrection.
Explain why admitting the possibility of supernatural events does not require endorsing every miracle report or its surrounding religious system.

routes.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not warrant concluding that Jesus physically rose because its bodily character, independence, corroboration, and comparative force remain uncertain and plausible alternatives persist.
routes.successCriteria: Demonstrate that visionary development, source limitations, natural tomb explanations, and comparable rival testimony prevent the cited considerations from specifically establishing a physical resurrection.

motionBridge.description: Show that the historical record does not make a physical resurrection sufficiently specific or warranted among the available explanations.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Pauline and Gospel materials do not unambiguously preserve firsthand testimony to ordinary physical encounters with the risen Jesus.
Provide historically plausible burial, reburial, theft, or narrative-development accounts that prevent a missing body from uniquely indicating resurrection.
Show that comparable miracle and witness traditions create a consistency test that the resurrection evidence must satisfy without selective standards.
Separate sincere belief, persecution, conversion, and visionary experience from firsthand knowledge of a physical resurrection and death specifically for that testimony.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify the absence or limits of independent, identifiable, and contemporaneous corroboration for the reported postmortem appearances.
Test whether the narrated burial authorization, tomb placement, and discovery details fit the relevant historical and narrative circumstances.

sections.title: Bodily Character and Development of the Appearance Traditions
sections.rationale: The motion requires a physical resurrection, so the meaning of Pauline bodily language, Gospel physicality, retained wounds, recognition scenes, and possible visionary development determines what event the sources purport to support.

sections.title: Appearances, Corroboration, and Explanatory Inference
sections.rationale: Individual and group encounter reports, the five hundred, Paul and James, companion corroboration, and the early proclamation form the principal testimonial basis for comparing resurrection with visionary or developmental explanations.

sections.title: Empty Tomb, Burial History, and Natural Alternatives
sections.rationale: The tomb is the principal proposed link between appearance testimony and a physically absent corpse, making burial plausibility, women witnesses, apologetic features, reburial, theft, and grave-disturbance alternatives burden-relevant.

sections.title: Rival Miracle Claims and Consistent Evidential Standards
sections.rationale: Mormon witnesses, Brigham Young's reported transfiguration, later Christian miracles, and possible non-Christian wonders test whether the historical criteria used for resurrection testimony distinguish it from structurally similar claims.

sections.title: Sincerity, Persecution, and Martyrdom Evidence
sections.rationale: Costly proclamation can bear on witness sincerity, but its force depends on the historical basis for apostolic danger or death and on whether the relevant people possessed firsthand bodily knowledge rather than visionary conviction.

routes.description: Establish that a simple divine agent provides a better cumulative explanation than naturalism of the universe, uniform laws, life-permitting conditions, embodied conscious agents, and the relevant modal structure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism has a sufficiently stronger combination of comparative prior simplicity and evidential likelihood across the disputed phenomena to be more probable than naturalism.

motionBridge.description: Connect the combined prior and likelihood case to the conclusion that theism is more probable than naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Supply an objective account of simplicity under which one essentially unlimited divine agent can receive a favorable comparative prior.
Show that uniform laws and life-permitting cosmic conditions are more expected given divine reasons than given an uncreated physical reality.
Show that embodied conscious agents with morally significant freedom are expected products of divine goodness and resist an equally simple naturalistic explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Justify applying predictive fit, comparative likelihood, and simplicity as rational explanatory criteria beyond ordinary scientific cases.
Defend a modal framework broad enough to compare the actual universe with alternative possible universes and ultimate explanations.

routes.description: Prevent theism from gaining a comparative probability advantage by supplying economical naturalistic accounts and challenging the claimed objectivity, likelihood advantage, and modal basis of the theistic comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalism remains at least as simple and explanatorily adequate as theism, or if the relevant priors, likelihoods, and modal alternatives do not warrant the claimed comparative probability ordering.

motionBridge.description: Connect naturalistic adequacy and underdetermination in the comparison to denial that theism is more probable than naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Provide a simple naturalistic initial reality and laws capable of explaining subsequent cosmic data without adding a divine agent.
Challenge whether the observed universe, especially its particular contents and production of humans, is more expected under theism.
Show that consciousness can be accommodated through identity theory or another natural emergence account without a decisive theistic advantage.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Frame the dispute as a comparison of equally detailed rivals across priors and the likelihood of the total partitioned evidence.
Ground modal claims in what exists and must exist rather than in conceivability, rational belief, or measures of ignorance.

sections.title: Comparative Method, Simplicity, and Priors
sections.rationale: The probability comparison depends on how explanatory fit and simplicity determine comparative priors, whether qualitative Bayesian dominance is available, and whether adding God unifies data or merely adds complexity.

sections.title: Cosmic Origins, Laws, and Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: The central cosmic clash concerns whether uniform laws and life-permitting conditions favor purposive divine creation or can follow from an economical naturalistic initial state and its dispositions.

sections.title: Divine Reasons, Anthropocentrism, and Embodied Agency
sections.rationale: Theism's likelihood claim relies on divine reasons to create finite embodied agents, while the comparison must address alternative creations, anthropocentric selection, and what embodiment contributes to morally significant interaction.

sections.title: Consciousness and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: Consciousness affects explanatory scope because the dispute tests whether privileged access defeats mind-brain identity and whether nonphysical minds could nevertheless arise within naturalism.

sections.title: Modality, Necessity, and Ultimate Explanation
sections.rationale: Accounts of possibility and necessity determine the admissible hypothesis space and whether God, laws, or an initial physical state can function as the ultimate unexplained reality.

routes.description: Establish that beginning evidence and life-permitting cosmic conditions create explanatory demands that naturalistic early-universe models do not discharge as well as a transcendent intelligent cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cosmological evidence supports a beginning or otherwise leaves model-dependent contingency, fine-tuning is a genuine feature requiring explanation, and intelligent agency provides a comparatively adequate cause of both origin and life-permitting order.

motionBridge.description: Connect modern cosmological evidence to a comparative explanatory preference for transcendent intelligent agency over naturalistic early-universe accounts.

centralBridges.description: Show that expansion evidence and relevant cosmological theorems provide reasonable support for a finite cosmic past or boundary requiring explanation.
Establish that life-permitting constants and initial conditions occupy meaningfully constrained ranges and are not fixed by an adequate deeper natural mechanism.
Show that a transcendent volitional intelligence has the causal attributes and known explanatory relevance needed to account for cosmic origin and fine-tuning.
Demonstrate that bounce, quantum-cosmological, inflationary, string, or multiverse proposals retain unexplained assumptions, information, or prior fine-tuning.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend inference to the best explanation and empirical expectations as legitimate standards even where direct observation or deductive proof is unavailable.
Support the compatibility of theistic commitments with scientific inquiry by relating theological ideas to natural law, intelligibility, and empirical investigation.

routes.description: Establish that current cosmology does not warrant an absolute beginning or a reliable fine-tuning probability and that testable naturalistic research remains preferable to an underdetermined design inference.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if beginning arguments outrun hot-Big-Bang observations and theorem scope, fine-tuning or its probabilities remain unsettled, physical alternatives retain legitimate empirical promise, and the proposed designer lacks distinctive causal or predictive support.

motionBridge.description: Show that modern cosmology underdetermines theism or intelligent design relative to naturalistic early-universe models and continued scientific agnosticism.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish evidence for a hot dense early universe from evidence for a singularity or absolute beginning, accounting for quantum-gravity limitations.
Establish that bounce, inflationary, quantum, necessity, or multiverse approaches remain legitimate candidates when judged by mathematical development and testable consequences.
Challenge whether cosmic constants have a justified possibility space and probability distribution sufficient to ground an improbability-based fine-tuning inference.
Show that a transcendent designer requires unsupported extrapolation from embodied minds and lacks sufficiently discriminating intentions, expectations, or predictions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require calibrated uncertainty where observations cannot distinguish global early-universe histories and current models depend on incomplete physics.
Contextualize science as a cross-cultural enterprise explainable through observable regularities and inquiry without a uniquely theological foundation.

sections.title: Scientific and Theological Standards of Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue establishes whether theological commitments can ground scientific expectations and whether cosmological explanation should admit theistic inference or remain restricted to developing, testable physical accounts.

sections.title: Evidence for a Cosmic Beginning
sections.rationale: The distinction between a hot early universe, a spacetime boundary, and an absolute beginning bears directly on whether cosmology supplies the origin premise required by the beginning-based theistic route.

sections.title: Early-Universe Models, Theorem Scope, and Uncertainty
sections.rationale: Bounce, quantum-cosmological, inflationary, and other pre-Big-Bang proposals determine whether naturalism has legitimate alternatives and whether their assumptions relocate rather than resolve the explanatory burden.

sections.title: Reality and Probability of Cosmic Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: The design inference requires defensible life-permitting ranges, contingency, and probabilistic significance, while the opposing route can resist the inference by disputing the measure, mechanism, or need for explanation.

sections.title: Design, Multiverse, Agency, and Predictive Expectations
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on comparative explanation: whether agency, naturalistic universe-generating mechanisms, or agnosticism better accounts for the relevant conditions under standards of causal adequacy, simplicity, and empirical expectation.

routes.description: Establish the anti-theist charge by arguing that religious claims lack adequate evidential foundations and that purported divine authority predictably corrupts moral judgment, personal autonomy, public institutions, and natural explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting the falsity or explanatory redundancy of supernatural claims to distinctive mechanisms of harm, while showing that morality, charity, and solidarity remain available without religion and therefore do not offset or validate those mechanisms.

motionBridge.description: Show that religion adds false supernatural authority to human affairs and thereby produces pervasive harms without supplying indispensable goods.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that naturalistic explanations better account for religious diversity, human origins, calamity, and religious texts than supernatural claims do.
Show how claims of divine authorization insulate coercion, theocracy, violence, bodily regulation, and subordination from ordinary moral correction.
Establish that innate solidarity and secular agency adequately support morality, charity, courage, and social reform without supernatural motivation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test Christianity's historical and moral credibility through disputed biblical narratives, miracle claims, inherited guilt, and divinely commanded violence.
Use civic, medical, and sectarian consequences to illustrate the practical operation of religious authority and belief.

routes.description: Defeat the sweeping indictment by presenting Christianity as a historically credible account of creation, fallenness, rescue, grace, and redemption whose adherents and institutions can produce charity, reform, civic goods, and transformed lives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if substantial religious good defeats the universal poison charge and if Christian grace supplies a coherent source of forgiveness and transformation, while objections from religious wrongdoing, secular morality, and disputed history receive burden-relevant answers.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity cannot be wholly poisonous because grace and Christian commitment produce material moral, personal, civic, and charitable goods.

centralBridges.description: Require the anti-theist charge to account consistently for religious benefits as well as harms rather than defining beneficial conduct as nonreligious by default.
Explain Christianity's core as undeserved rescue and forgiveness capable of sustaining repentance, sacrificial love, and personal transformation.
Defend the historical and explanatory credibility of Christian belief against claims that scripture, creation, and miracles are merely ignorant inventions.
Connect Christian conviction to durable charitable, reformist, medical, educational, and constitutional contributions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Contextualize difficult biblical violence and distinguish Christianity's central teaching from every act performed under a religious label.
Use secular oppression and inherited moral capital to challenge claims that removing religion eliminates poison or fully explains present moral norms.

sections.title: Scope of the Poison Charge and Attribution of Good and Harm
sections.rationale: Defines the motion-level burden and tests how religious motives should be attributed when believers perform charitable acts, commit harms, or participate in conduct also available to nonbelievers.

sections.title: Religious Truth, Naturalistic Explanation, and Historical Credibility
sections.rationale: Addresses whether supernatural creation, miracles, and scripture possess credible evidential support or whether evolution, religious diversity, and ordinary causation make divine agency unnecessary.

sections.title: Divine Authority, Scriptural Morality, and Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Covers the proposed mechanism by which divine commands may authorize coercion, violence, surveillance, and subordination, together with contextual defenses of biblical teaching and conduct.

sections.title: Secular Morality, Christian Grace, and Personal Transformation
sections.rationale: Tests whether morality and compassion arise independently from human solidarity or depend on common grace and inherited Christian formation, and whether forgiveness produces distinctive reform.

sections.title: Charity, Civic Institutions, and Social Consequences
sections.rationale: Compares claims about religious service, abolition, education, liberty, medicine, theocracy, sectarian conflict, and secular oppression as practical consequences bearing on the motion.
